newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Commonwealth split on climate change.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth split on climate change.

text.p: Commonwealth countries urged the U.N. Earth Summit on Wednesday to respond urgently to the needs of small island nations but they could not agree on the islands' biggest concern, global warming.

In a document released by Australian Environment Minister Robert Hill, the ministers from the Commonwealth agreed that "climate change and sea-level rise were critical issues requiring urgent global response."
But they acknowledged they were split on how to reduce pollution from burning fossil fuels that is warming the planet and raising sea levels.

Facing the threat of being swamped by the oceans and more severe storms, the small island nations that comprise about half the Commonwealth want industrial countries to cut carbon emissions by 20 percent by 2010.
But Australia, which relies largely on coal power, has balked at setting targets.
The ministers were also split on whether to pursue an international convention on protecting forests, which has been one of the more contentious issues at the summit.
They said recommendations of a U.N. intergovernmental panel on forests should be carried out without delay, but more discussion was needed on pursuing a legally binding agreement on forests.
The United States, backed by most major environmental groups, is against negotiating a new treaty, while Canada, the European Union and other countries are in favour.
